suggestions.title: The Godfather Part II
suggestions.description: The highest-rated film you have never been shown — 9.0 on IMDb, and the only sequel until Return of the King to win Best Picture. Coppola cuts between two timelines: Robert De Niro's young Vito Corleone arriving in a crowded 1901 New York and building the family's power from nothing, and Al Pacino's Michael in 1958 - colder, greyer, more alone with every scene — expanding the empire into Las Vegas, Hollywood and pre-revolutionary Cuba, and slowly discovering which of his own family is working against him. The structure is the point: every time you warm to the immigrant father, the film cuts back to the son he would not recognise. Gordon Willis shot the two eras in deliberately different registers — warm amber and sepia for Vito, cool desaturated blues and shadows for Michael — and Nino Rota's score carries it. De Niro won an Oscar for a performance that is roughly 60% Sicilian dialogue, Pacino gives the most tightly coiled work of his career, and the Fredo confrontation on the dock at Lake Tahoe is the moment the film stops being a crime epic and becomes a study of how power eats a family from the inside. You have seen Part I (Godfather, 1972); this is 202 minutes that pay it off.

suggestions.title: Psycho
suggestions.description: Of the 93 films in your history you have never been shown a single Hitchcock — and this is the one that rewrote the rules. Hitchcock financed it himself for around $800,000, shot it in black and white with the crew from his TV show to keep it cheap, and then did the thing nobody expected: he killed his biggest star (Janet Leigh) about a third of the way in and let the audience watch the film collapse into a completely different story about a shy young man named Norman Bates. Bernard Herrmann's score is strings only, and the 45-second shower scene — 78 camera setups, roughly 52 cuts, a knife that never actually touches skin — remains the most analysed sequence in the medium; the shower scene is not shocking because of gore, it is shocking because of editing. Watch it as the ancestor of everything you have already seen: the dread in The Shining, the silence before the reveal in Get Out, the family rot in Hereditary. The staged psychiatrist monologue at the end is the one piece that has aged, and it is worth forgiving to see the source. Anthony Perkins' performance holds the whole thing together — a man doing a perfect impression of normality while you slowly realise he is the film's only real monster.

suggestions.title: Toy Story 3
suggestions.description: The payoff to the 1995 film you have already been shown — and a genuine heist-and-escape picture wearing a family-film costume. Andy is leaving for college, the toys face the bin or the attic, a mix-up lands them at Sunnyside Daycare, and Pixar quietly rebuilds The Great Escape in a room full of toddlers: census-taking prisoners, a corrupt warden (Ned Beatty's strawberry-scented Lotso), a rec room that becomes a cell block, and an escape plan that hinges on knowing which toy is the one who reports on everyone else. It is the only Toy Story film with real stakes, and the staging of the incinerator sequence — the gang holding hands and going still, then the claw — is Pixar's single best moment of pure cinema, played without dialogue at all. The ending, which I will not spoil, is the reason adults cry at this one: it is a film about being outgrown, told from the perspective of the people who get outgrown. Academically it is also the first animated film to gross over $1 billion and it won two Oscars (Best Animated Feature, Best Original Song). Genre shift from the last two rounds: this one is fun.
